lead: A residual property is the gap between a real-fluid property and its ideal-gas value at the same temperature and pressure. Real gases deviate from ideal behaviour, so ideal-gas formulas alone give wrong enthalpy, entropy and Gibbs energy. The residual isolates that deviation. It is used with cubic equations of state and generalized correlations to get compressor power, throttle effects, heat-exchanger duties and fugacity coefficients. Once the residual is known, add it to the ideal-gas value at the same T and P. This chapter shows the defining integrals and one worked calculation.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.2 for exact differentials, the compressibility factor Z from Unit 2, and the fugacity coefficient from Unit 5.

sections.h3: Definition at fixed T and P

blocks.text: At temperature T and pressure P, a real fluid has molar property M. The ideal gas at the same T and P has molar property M^ig. The residual property is M^R = M − M^ig. M can be V, U, H, S, G or A; the units follow M. The definition uses the same T and P because that fixes one comparison state for both fluids. The ideal gas is a reference, not a second real state.

blocks.where: M is any molar property at T and P; M^ig is the ideal-gas value at the same T and P; M^R is the residual property.

blocks.text: For an ideal gas, U^ig and H^ig depend only on T. S^ig and G^ig also depend on P, through S^ig(T,P) = S^ig(T,P°) − R ln(P/P°) and G^ig = H^ig − T S^ig. The pressure terms cancel in some residuals and remain in others. Every residual property of an ideal gas is zero. As P → 0, H^R, S^R, G^R, A^R and U^R tend to zero. V^R is different: V^R = (Z − 1)RT/P tends to B, the second virial coefficient, a finite value, because V and V^ig both diverge while their difference stays finite.

blocks.where: V^R is residual molar volume (m³/mol); Z = PV/RT is compressibility factor; R = 8.314 J/(mol K); T is temperature (K); P is pressure (Pa).

blocks.text: Negative V^R means the real gas occupies less volume than the ideal gas at the same T and P. Attractive forces usually cause this at moderate pressure.

For a pure fluid, the fugacity coefficient is φ = f/P, where f is fugacity and P is pressure. Unit 5 develops φ fully. The residual Gibbs energy is tied to it by G^R = RT ln φ. The integrated form uses the compressibility factor Z = PV/RT.

blocks.where: G^R is residual molar Gibbs energy (J/mol); R = 8.314 J/(mol K); T is absolute temperature (K); φ is fugacity coefficient; Z = PV/RT; P is pressure (Pa).

blocks.text: At P → 0, (Z − 1)/P tends to a finite limit, the pressure virial coefficient B′, so the integral remains finite. If φ < 1, then ln φ < 0 and G^R is negative: the real gas has lower Gibbs energy than the ideal gas at that T and P. If φ > 1, G^R is positive; φ = 1 gives G^R = 0. This sign check catches many calculation errors. The same integral also gives the fugacity coefficient used in phase equilibrium; see Unit 5 and Unit 6.
At constant T, the fundamental relation for enthalpy gives dH = [V − T(∂V/∂T)_P] dP. Integrate from zero pressure, where the gas is ideal, to pressure P.

blocks.where: H^R is residual molar enthalpy (J/mol); V is molar volume (m³/mol); T is temperature (K); (∂V/∂T)_P is the temperature derivative of V at constant pressure; P is pressure (Pa).

blocks.text: For an ideal gas, V = RT/P and T(∂V/∂T)_P = RT/P. The bracket is zero, so H^R = 0, as required. For a cubic equation of state, substitute V(T,P) and integrate. The result is a closed-form departure function.
Entropy follows from dS = −(∂V/∂T)_P dP at constant T. With M^R = M − M^ig, the residual is:

blocks.where: S^R is residual molar entropy (J/(mol K)); R = 8.314 J/(mol K); P is pressure (Pa); V is molar volume (m³/mol); (∂V/∂T)_P is at constant pressure.

blocks.text: The ideal-gas part is R/P, so the integrand vanishes for an ideal gas. The three residuals are consistent through G^R = H^R − T S^R. Cubic equations of state such as van der Waals, Redlich-Kwong and Peng-Robinson supply V(T,P) and its temperature derivative. Generalized correlations use reduced temperature Tr = T/Tc, reduced pressure Pr = P/Pc and acentric factor ω. They tabulate H^R/RTc and S^R/R. The values feed compressor power, valve throttling and heat-exchanger duties.

spec.title: Residual property as a departure
spec.aria: The real-gas property and the ideal-gas property at 300 K and 50 bar are compared; their difference is the residual property.

examples.question: At 300 K and 50 bar, a pure gas has fugacity coefficient φ = 0.90. Calculate its residual molar Gibbs energy G^R. Use R = 8.314 J/(mol K).
steps: Write the relation: G^R = RT ln φ.
examples.answer: G^R = −262.8 J/mol; the real gas has lower Gibbs energy than the ideal gas at 300 K and 50 bar.
examples.check:
import math
R = 8.314
T = 300.0
phi = 0.90
GR = R * T * math.log(phi)
print(round(GR, 1))

code.code:
import math
R = 8.314
T = 300.0
phi = 0.90
GR = R * T * math.log(phi)
print(round(GR, 1))

traps: Using the same temperature and volume instead of the same temperature and pressure. Residual properties are defined at the same T and P.
Thinking an ideal gas has nonzero residual enthalpy or entropy at high pressure. Every M^R for an ideal gas is zero.
Dropping the sign of ln φ. φ < 1 gives negative G^R; φ > 1 gives positive G^R.
Forgetting the sign in S^R. With M^R = M − M^ig, write S^R = ∫₀^P [R/P − (∂V/∂T)_P] dP.
Using bar in V^R = (Z − 1)RT/P. Convert pressure to Pa so R in J/(mol K) gives m³/mol; 1 bar = 10⁵ Pa.

quiz.q: Define residual property M^R for a pure fluid.
quiz.a: M^R = M(T,P) − M^ig(T,P), at the same temperature T and pressure P. M can be V, U, H, S, G or A.

quiz.q: Why is every residual property of an ideal gas zero?
quiz.a: Because the real-fluid property and the ideal-gas property are then the same at the same T and P; their difference is zero by definition.

quiz.q: At 300 K and 50 bar, Z = 0.90. Calculate V^R in cm³/mol. Use R = 8.314 J/(mol K), 1 bar = 10⁵ Pa.
Explain why H^R uses V − T(∂V/∂T)_P rather than V − V^ig alone.
quiz.a: At constant T, dH = [V − T(∂V/∂T)_P] dP. V − V^ig alone would vanish for an ideal gas, but it gives the wrong residual enthalpy for a real gas. The correct integrand is V − T(∂V/∂T)_P, which cancels for an ideal gas because V^ig = T(∂V^ig/∂T)_P = RT/P. The derivative term accounts for how attraction and repulsion change with temperature.

quiz.q: A gas at 300 K has φ = 0.90 and H^R = −500 J/mol. Find S^R.
Write the relation between G^R and fugacity coefficient φ.
quiz.a: G^R = RT ln φ, or G^R/RT = ln φ = ∫₀^P (Z − 1) dP/P.

quiz.q: For φ < 1, what is the sign of G^R, and what does it mean physically?
quiz.a: ln φ < 0, so G^R < 0. The real gas has lower Gibbs energy than the ideal gas at the same T and P; it is more stable than the ideal-gas reference by that amount.

quiz.q: Why must residual properties compare real and ideal gas at the same T and P, not the same T and V?
quiz.a: The chosen T and P fix the state for both fluids; ideal-gas H and G at that state are then well defined. At the same T and V, the pressures differ, so the difference mixes pressure and volume effects and is not the residual property used in property relations.

beyond: Not for the exam. Process simulators store residual enthalpy and entropy as departure functions for every stream. Compressor and turbine vendors use them to get shaft power from cubic equations of state. The same integrals appear in CO₂ capture, LNG cold-box design and supercritical extraction. Search 'enthalpy departure function', 'Peng-Robinson departure functions' and 'Lee-Kesler tables'.
